region: Pacific side of Central America, from Panama to southwestern Mexico
description: Cocobolo is a very dense, oily Central American rosewood whose heartwood turns deep orange-red with dark streaks. It is prized for knife and tool handles, inlay, turned boxes, pens and musical instruments; its natural oils help it polish well but make gluing harder.

hazards.summary: Several patch-test-confirmed reports show cocobolo can cause allergic skin rashes in woodworkers and in people using cocobolo items such as recorders and bracelets. In one case a cabinetmaker developed a rash over most of the body after working with the sawdust.
An early report described respiratory allergy, including asthma, in workers exposed to cocobolo dust. We could not confirm what testing was done, so treat this as a reported effect.
All wood dust is classified as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancers of the nose and sinuses after long-term exposure. This applies to this wood like any other.

exposure_limits.note: Applies to wood dust generally; this species has no separate ACGIH value.

known_compounds.name: obtusaquinone
known_compounds.role: quinone methide identified as the main skin sensitizer

known_compounds.name: R-4-methoxydalbergione
known_compounds.role: dalbergione that gave positive patch tests in sensitized patients

related_species_note: Cocobolo is one of the Dalbergia rosewoods; see also rosewood (genus) and Brazilian rosewood. Dalbergia woods share related quinone allergens, and reactions to more than one Dalbergia wood have been reported (Gamboa-2024).

notes_internal: Eaton-1973 has no abstract on PubMed; species and outcome taken from Schlunssen-2018 table ('Cocobolla / Palisander, Dalbergia retusa, RS OA'). Upgrade respiratory hazard to level 1 only if full text shows challenge/skin/sIgE testing. HSE-WIS30 lists 'Rosewood (many species)' but does not name cocobolo, so it is not cited here (decide whether the rosewood row should apply). Jensen 2016 (PMID 26251338) and Leider 1950 (PMID 15426324) are further cocobolo dermatitis reports, not added (no abstracts read). Common names other than cocobolo are from the FPL sheet; 'granadillo' is used for several other woods.
